question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
One of them who were hidings at the back of a rock fired at the villagers.
option_1: one of them who were hiding behind a rock
option_2: one of them who was hide behind a rock
option_3: one of them who hiding behind a rock
option_4: one of them who was hiding behind a rock
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. one of them who was hiding behind a rock.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the relative clause is "who", referring back to "one" (singular) — not to "them" (plural). Since the antecedent is singular, the verb after "who" must also be singular: "was", not "were".

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense: Subject + was/were + V1+ing. For a singular subject, use "was"; for a plural subject, use "were". The correct continuous form of the verb "hide" is "hiding" (not the ungrammatical noun-like form "hidings" used in the original sentence).

• Applying the rule: "one" (singular) + "was" + "hiding" + "behind" a rock. The preposition "behind" (meaning at the back of) is idiomatically preferred over the wordier "at the back of".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "were hiding behind a rock" is incorrect because it uses the plural auxiliary "were", which does not agree with the singular antecedent "one".

• Option 2: "was hide behind a rock" is incorrect because "hide" is used in its bare base form after "was"; the continuous tense requires the -ing form, "hiding".

• Option 3: "hiding behind a rock" is incorrect because it drops the auxiliary verb "was" altogether, leaving the clause without a proper finite verb.

NOTE

• Remember: in a relative clause beginning with "one of + plural noun + who", the verb agrees with "one" (singular), e.g., "She is one of the girls who was praised" — not "were".

• Common SSC trap: "-ing" forms used as nouns (e.g., "hidings", "runnings") are usually wrong when a continuous verb form is required; always check whether an auxiliary + V-ing pattern is needed.

question:
Select the word which means the same as the group of words underlined in the given sentence.
I can't believe that I am doing this ordinary and dull task.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Mundane.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Mundane" means lacking interest or excitement; dull, ordinary and commonplace, which is exactly what "ordinary and dull" conveys. (सांसारिक/नीरस)
◦ Example: Filing paperwork is one of the most mundane tasks in the office.

• The word comes from the Latin "mundanus" (of the world), originally meaning "worldly" as opposed to "spiritual", and later came to mean "ordinary/routine".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Immoral (अनैतिक): Not conforming to accepted standards of morality; wicked. This has no connection to "ordinary and dull".

• Option 2: Tenacious (दृढ़): Holding firmly to something; persistent. This describes determination, not dullness.

• Option 4: Destitute (निराश्रित): Extremely poor, lacking the necessities of life. This is unrelated to the meaning of "ordinary and dull".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "mundane": humdrum, routine, monotonous, tedious, banal, prosaic.

• Do not confuse "mundane" (dull/ordinary) with "mundane" used loosely for "worldly" — in modern usage on competitive exams, it almost always tests the "boring/ordinary" sense.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in superlative degree of comparison.
It was probably the happy afternoon of her life.
option_1: This afternoon of her life was the happy.
option_2: It was an happier afternoon in their life before that.
option_4: It was probably the happiest afternoon of her life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. It was probably the happiest afternoon of her life.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence uses the positive degree adjective "happy" incorrectly with the definite article "the", which signals that a superlative form is intended ("the happy afternoon" is not grammatically complete/correct).

• Rule — Degrees of Comparison: Positive: happy; Comparative: happier (+ than); Superlative: the + happiest (used to compare more than two things, here "this afternoon" against all other afternoons of her life).

• Applying the rule: "happy" → superlative → "happiest", retaining the article "the" already present. The rest of the sentence structure ("It was probably... of her life") stays unchanged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it awkwardly rearranges the sentence and leaves "the happy" incomplete — an adjective without a noun or proper superlative ending, which is ungrammatical.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it changes the degree to comparative ("happier") instead of superlative, and also wrongly changes "her" to "their", altering the meaning of the original sentence.

• Option 3 ("No change needed") is incorrect because the original sentence is grammatically wrong as it stands — "the happy afternoon" needs the superlative "-est" form to be correct.

NOTE

• Superlative adjectives of one or two syllables usually take "-est" (happy → happiest, big → biggest); adjectives of three or more syllables use "most" (beautiful → most beautiful).

• Watch for the definite article "the" immediately before an adjective — it is a strong signal that the superlative degree is required.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
P. but results in widespread hunger, death and social unrest
Q. some of the causes of famine in that region
R. drought, floods, war and economic instability are
S. which not only causes severe shortage of food
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. RQSP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every jumbled-sentence question has one part that logically must come first — the part that introduces the subject of the sentence. Here, R ("drought, floods, war and economic instability are") introduces the subject list and must open the sentence, since P, Q and S all depend grammatically on something stated earlier.

• Rule: Identify the independent subject-introducing clause first, then trace the pronoun/conjunction links — "which" in S must refer back to a noun just mentioned (here, "famine", from Q), and "but" in P must connect two contrasting/continuing ideas.

• Applying the rule: R (subject) → Q ("...are some of the causes of famine in that region") → S ("which not only causes severe shortage of food") → P ("but results in widespread hunger, death and social unrest"). This gives the coherent sentence: "Drought, floods, war and economic instability are some of the causes of famine in that region, which not only causes severe shortage of food but results in widespread hunger, death and social unrest."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (RSQP) is incorrect because it places S ("which not only causes...") directly after R, before "famine" has even been mentioned in Q — the relative pronoun "which" would have nothing to refer to.

• Option 3 (QRSP) is incorrect because it starts with Q, which begins with the verb-less fragment "some of the causes of famine in that region" — this cannot logically open the sentence without R's subject preceding it.

• Option 4 (QPSR) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 3 (wrong opening part), and additionally reverses the logical order of S and P, breaking the "not only...but" correlative structure.

NOTE

• In "not only...but (also)" constructions, the two linked clauses must stay adjacent and in that fixed order — a strong clue for sequencing parts correctly.

• Always look for a part with no pronoun or connector at all to identify the likely opening part, and match pronouns like "which/it/this" to their nearest preceding noun.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The ______ age for retirement is 65 years in India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Mandatory.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Mandatory" — required by law or rule; compulsory.

• Spelling key: MAN + DA + TORY. The word derives from the Latin "mandatum" (something commanded), the same root as "mandate" and "command". Remembering the base word "mandate" helps fix the spelling of "mandatory".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Mendatory" — incorrect; the first syllable is wrongly spelt "men" instead of "man".

• Option 2: "Mendetory" — incorrect; both the first syllable ("men" instead of "man") and the second syllable ("de" instead of "da") are wrong.

• Option 3: "Mendaytory" — incorrect; the first syllable is wrongly spelt "men" instead of "man", and an extra "y" is inserted after "da".

NOTE

• Related words: mandate (noun/verb), mandatorily (adverb).

• Do not confuse "mandatory" (compulsory) with "voluntary" (optional) — a commonly tested antonym pair.

• Other commonly confused "-ory/-ary" spellings in SSC exams: statutory, obligatory, discretionary, complimentary, complementary.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
The news is very good to be true.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. "very good".

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the structure "very + adjective + to + infinitive", which is grammatically wrong here. The intended meaning — that the news is so good that it seems unbelievable — requires the "too...to" construction, not "very...to".

• Rule: "Too + adjective + to + verb" is used to show that something is excessive to the point of an undesirable or surprising result (e.g., "too good to be true", "too hot to drink"). "Very" simply intensifies an adjective and cannot be followed by a "to-infinitive" of result in this way.

• Applying the rule: "The news is very good to be true" must be corrected to "The news is too good to be true". The error therefore lies in the segment "very good", which should read "too good".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "to be true" is correct as printed; it correctly completes the "too...to" idiom once "very" is corrected to "too".

• Option 3: "The news" is correct; "news" is an uncountable noun that always takes a singular verb, which is properly used here.

• Option 4: "is" is correct; it agrees correctly with the singular uncountable subject "news".

NOTE

• Common idiom: "too good to be true" — used when something seems so favourable that it is hard to believe.

• Do not confuse "too...to" (excessive, negative result) with "so...that" (so good that I couldn't believe it) — both are correct but structurally different; "very...to" is never correct.

• "News" is always singular in English, unlike its plural-looking form (e.g., "The news is good", not "are good").

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a spelling error.
They need to / wave the participation / fees for people / with disabilities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. "wave the participation".

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "wave" is a spelling error in this context. The intended word is "waive", meaning to voluntarily give up or refrain from insisting on a right, claim or requirement.

• Rule — commonly confused homophone-like pair: "Wave" (to move to and fro, or a swell of water) versus "Waive" (to forgo/relinquish, especially a fee, rule or right). The context — "the participation fees" — clearly calls for "waive", since fees are being given up/excused, not physically moved.

• Corrected sentence: "They need to waive the participation fees for people with disabilities."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "with disabilities." is correctly spelt and grammatically fine as the concluding segment.

• Option 3: "fees for people" is correctly spelt; no error here.

• Option 4: "They need to" is correctly spelt; no error here.

NOTE

• Other commonly confused SSC spelling/word pairs: "stationary" (not moving) vs "stationery" (writing materials); "principal" (head/main) vs "principle" (rule); "complement" (to complete) vs "compliment" (praise).

• Remember "waive" like "waiver" (a document giving up a right/claim) to fix the spelling in memory.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined segment.
The child was not guilty of any wrongdoing and lacked knowledge or awareness of wrongdoing.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Innocent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Innocent" means not guilty of a crime or wrongdoing; free from moral wrong; lacking awareness or experience of evil, which precisely matches the underlined phrase "not guilty of any wrongdoing and lacked knowledge or awareness of wrongdoing". (निर्दोष/मासूम)
◦ Example: The court found the accused innocent of all charges.

• One-word substitution questions require identifying a single word that captures the entire meaning of the given phrase, without adding or losing meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Ignorant (अज्ञानी): Lacking knowledge or awareness in general. It captures only the "lacked knowledge" part but misses the crucial "not guilty of wrongdoing" sense, so it is an incomplete match.

• Option 2: Inexperienced (अनुभवहीन): Lacking experience or skill in something — this refers to lack of practice/skill, not to innocence regarding wrongdoing.

• Option 4: Cruel (क्रूर): Deliberately causing pain or suffering — this is the opposite in spirit of the innocent, blameless child described in the sentence.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes often confused with "innocent": "naive" (excessively trusting, lacking worldly experience), "gullible" (easily deceived), "guileless" (without deceit).

• "Innocent" is commonly tested opposite "guilty" — remember the pair for both synonym/antonym and one-word substitution questions.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. Looks first to his own profit
B. And then to the king's,
C. Or destroys the king's gain altogether
D. The chief collector of revenue
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. D, A, B, C.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence needs a clear subject before any verb can make sense. D ("The chief collector of revenue") is the only part that supplies a subject with no dangling pronoun or connector, so it must come first.

• Rule: After identifying the subject (D), find the part containing its main verb — A ("Looks first to his own profit") — which must follow directly since "Looks" needs a subject immediately before it. Then trace the connecting words: "And then" in B logically continues "Looks... to his own profit, and then to the king's", and "Or" in C offers the final alternative, so it comes last.

• Applying the rule: D (subject) → A (verb + first object) → B ("and then" continuation) → C ("or" alternative). Full sentence: "The chief collector of revenue looks first to his own profit, and then to the king's, or destroys the king's gain altogether."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (B, D, A, C) is incorrect because it opens with B ("And then to the king's,"), which begins with the connector "And then" — this cannot logically start a sentence with nothing preceding it.

• Option 3 (D, C, A, B) is incorrect because it places C ("Or destroys...") immediately after the subject D, before the first verb phrase A has even appeared — "or" needs a preceding alternative to contrast with.

• Option 4 (A, B, C, D) is incorrect because it begins with the verb phrase A ("Looks first...") without any subject at all, making the sentence grammatically incomplete at the start.

NOTE

• A useful strategy: look for the part that reads like a complete subject with no leading connector (and, or, which, but) — it almost always opens the sentence.

• Correlative-style structures like "first...and then...or" must retain their given internal order once the subject and verb are correctly placed.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of 'potential' in the given sentence.
I have seen Radhya growing in the last few years; she now has the capability to fight worse situations.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Capability.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Potential" means an inherent capacity or ability that may be developed and result in future success or usefulness. In the sentence, this matches the word "capability", meaning the power or ability to do something. (क्षमता/सामर्थ्य)
◦ Example: She has the potential/capability to become an excellent leader.

• This question asks you to find, from within the sentence itself, the word that already carries the meaning of "potential" — here, "capability" is used contextually to mean exactly that.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Worse" means of poorer quality or more severe — it is an adjective describing "situations", unrelated in meaning to "potential".

• Option 2: "Situations" refers to circumstances or conditions, not to an inherent ability, so it cannot be a synonym for "potential".

• Option 3: "Growing" refers to increasing or developing over time — it describes a process, not the underlying capacity or ability that "potential" denotes.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "potential": capacity, aptitude, promise, possibility.

• Do not confuse "potential" (capacity for future development) with "potent" (powerful/effective) — both share the same root but differ in meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym for the given word.
Strength
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Power.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Strength" means the quality or state of being physically, mentally or emotionally strong; power or force. "Power" is its closest synonym among the given options. (शक्ति/ताकत)
◦ Example: His inner strength/power helped him overcome the setback.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Recluse" (एकांतवासी): A person who lives alone and avoids others — completely unrelated in meaning to "strength".

• Option 2: "Weakness" (कमजोरी): The direct antonym of "strength" (lack of strength/power), not a synonym.

• Option 4: "Disability" (अक्षमता): A physical or mental condition limiting a person's abilities — this is closer in spirit to "weakness" than to "strength", and is therefore incorrect.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "strength": vigour, might, robustness, potency, fortitude (for inner/mental strength).

• Antonym pair frequently tested: strength ↔ weakness/frailty/debility.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Feasibility
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Probability.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Feasibility" refers to the likelihood or possibility that a plan, task or idea can be successfully carried out. Among the given choices, "Probability" (the likelihood of something being the case or happening) is the closest available match, since both words revolve around the idea of "likelihood/possibility of something being achieved or true". (संभावना)
◦ Example: The team studied the feasibility/probability of completing the project on time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sustainability" (धारणीयता): The ability to be maintained or continued over the long term without depleting resources — a related but distinct concept from feasibility (which is about whether something can be done at all, not whether it can be maintained).

• Option 2: "Impropriety" (अनुचितता): Behaviour or conduct that fails to conform to accepted standards; unrelated in meaning to feasibility.

• Option 3: "Heavy" (भारी): Refers to weight or intensity; has no semantic connection to feasibility.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "feasibility": practicability, viability, workability, achievability.

• Do not confuse "feasibility" (whether something can be done) with "viability" (whether it can survive/succeed once done) — though closely related, SSC vocabulary lists often use them interchangeably as near-synonyms.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Would pizza or burger rather be eaten by you?
option_1: Would you rather eat pizza or burger?
option_2: Would you rather eaten pizza or burger?
option_3: Would you rather ate pizza or burger?
option_4: Would you eat pizza or burger?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Would you rather eat pizza or burger?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Would pizza or burger rather be eaten by you?" is in the passive voice, using the structure "would...rather be + V3 + by".

• Rule — "would rather" construction: Active: Subject + would rather + V1 (base form) + Object; Passive: Object + would rather be + V3 + by + Subject. The modal expression "would rather" is always followed by the bare infinitive (V1) in the active voice, never a past form or participle.

• Applying the rule: the object "pizza or burger" becomes the object of the active sentence; the agent "by you" becomes the subject "you"; and the past participle "eaten" reverts to its base form "eat", retaining the question structure.
◦ Active: Would you rather eat pizza or burger?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because it keeps the past participle "eaten" instead of changing it to the base form "eat", which "would rather" requires.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it uses the past tense form "ate" instead of the base form "eat"; "would rather" is never followed by a simple past verb.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it drops the word "rather" entirely, changing the structure and meaning of the original sentence.

NOTE

• "Would rather" is always followed by the base form of the verb (bare infinitive) when referring to one's own preference: "I would rather stay home."

• When "would rather" refers to a different subject's action, it is followed by the simple past ("I would rather you left now") — a distinct, more advanced construction not tested here.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
She's been beating around the bush all afternoon - I just wish she would come out and tell us what she really thinks.
option_1: avoiding to talk directly about a topic or issue
option_3: denying to have her head in the clouds
option_4: there to give the cold shoulder
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. avoiding to talk directly about a topic or issue.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "beating around the bush" means to avoid talking about what is important, or to delay giving a direct answer on an uncomfortable topic. (घुमा-फिराकर बात करना/मुद्दे को टालना)
◦ Example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what happened.

• The phrase originates from hunting, where beaters would strike bushes to drive out game without approaching the animal directly — hence "beating around" (rather than directly at) the target.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To be overprotective (अति-सुरक्षात्मक): To be excessively protective or careful about someone — unrelated to avoiding a direct answer.

• Option 3: To have one's head in the clouds (हवाई किले बनाना): To be unrealistic or day-dreaming, out of touch with reality — a different idiom altogether.

• Option 4: To give someone the cold shoulder (अनदेखा करना/उपेक्षा करना): To deliberately ignore or be unfriendly towards someone — describes coldness, not evasive talking.

NOTE

• Other idioms of evasiveness often tested by SSC: "to skirt around an issue", "to hedge one's bets", "to sit on the fence" (avoid taking a clear side).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Elaborate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Complex.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Elaborate" (as an adjective) means detailed and complicated in design or planning; intricate. "Complex" is its closest synonym among the given options. (जटिल/विस्तृत)
◦ Example: The wedding involved an elaborate/complex arrangement of decorations and ceremonies.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Easy" (आसान): Requiring little effort; simple to do — the near-opposite of "elaborate".

• Option 3: "Simple" (सरल): Plain, uncomplicated — an antonym, not a synonym, of "elaborate".

• Option 4: "Plain" (सादा): Ordinary, without decoration or embellishment — again close to the opposite of "elaborate", which implies intricate detail.

NOTE

• As a verb, "to elaborate" means to explain something in more detail ("Could you elaborate on that point?") — a distinct but related sense.

• Other synonyms of "elaborate" (adjective): intricate, ornate, detailed, complicated. Antonyms: simple, plain, basic.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
It's not polite to blow your own trumpet in front of others.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. brag one's own accomplishment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "blow your own trumpet" means to boast or talk proudly about one's own achievements and abilities. (अपनी प्रशंसा स्वयं करना/डींग हांकना)
◦ Example: He is always blowing his own trumpet about his promotion.

• The image is of a person literally playing a trumpet to announce their own arrival or achievements — hence the association with self-praise and boasting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To criticise someone unfairly (किसी की अनुचित आलोचना करना): To find fault with another person without good reason — unrelated to self-praise.

• Option 3: To play a musical instrument: This is the literal, non-idiomatic meaning of the individual words "blow" and "trumpet", not the intended figurative sense.

• Option 4: To give someone a compliment (किसी की प्रशंसा करना): This refers to praising another person, whereas the idiom is specifically about praising oneself.

NOTE

• Other idioms of self-praise/boasting: "to sing one's own praises", "to toot one's own horn" (American equivalent).

• Contrast with idioms of modesty: "to hide one's light under a bushel" (to be modest about one's talents).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined segment in the following sentence.
After the scandal, the king was left with no choice but to announce his act of renouncing the throne.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Abdication.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Abdication" means the act of formally giving up a throne, right, power or responsibility, which precisely matches "act of renouncing the throne". (राजगद्दी त्याग)
◦ Example: The king's abdication shocked the entire nation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Coronation (राज्याभिषेक): The ceremony of crowning a king or queen — the opposite process of taking up the throne, not giving it up.

• Option 2: Extradition (प्रत्यर्पण): The formal handing over of a person accused or convicted of a crime by one state/country to another — unrelated to giving up a throne.

• Option 3: Exoneration (दोषमुक्ति): Being officially cleared of blame or a criminal charge — has no connection to renouncing a throne.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: "abdicate" (verb, to give up the throne/responsibility formally); "resignation" (giving up a job or post, used for non-royal contexts).

• Do not confuse "abdication" (giving up power) with "abduction" (kidnapping) — words with similar-sounding prefixes but unrelated meanings.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Ambivalent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Unequivocal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ambivalent" means having mixed or contradictory feelings or attitudes towards someone/something; uncertain or unable to decide. Its antonym, "Unequivocal", means leaving no doubt; clear and certain in meaning. (स्पष्ट/असंदिग्ध — the opposite of अनिर्णीत/दुविधाग्रस्त)
◦ Example: Unlike her ambivalent feelings about the job, his support for the plan was completely unequivocal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Unpredictable" (अप्रत्याशित): Not able to be predicted; this describes uncertainty about future events, not a clear opposite of "mixed feelings" — in fact it leans closer in spirit to ambivalence than away from it.

• Option 2: "Legitimate" (वैध): Conforming to the law or to accepted standards; unrelated to certainty of feeling or opinion.

• Option 4: "Irresistible" (अनूठा/अप्रतिरोध्य): Too attractive or powerful to be resisted; describes appeal, not decisiveness or clarity of feeling.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "ambivalent": uncertain, torn, indecisive, conflicted. Other antonyms: certain, decisive, clear-cut, definite.

• Do not confuse "ambivalent" (having mixed feelings) with "ambiguous" (having more than one possible meaning, used for statements/language, not feelings).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The package was delivered by the courier to the recipient's doorstep.
option_1: The recipient received the package delivered by the courier.
option_2: The package was being delivered by the courier to the recipient's doorstep.
option_3: The courier delivered the package to the recipient's doorstep.
option_4: The package was delivered to the recipient's doorstep by the courier.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The courier delivered the package to the recipient's doorstep.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The package was delivered by the courier to the recipient's doorstep" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense, using the structure "Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject".

• Rule — Simple Past Tense: Active: Subject + V2 + Object; Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject.

• Applying the rule: the agent "the courier" (after "by") becomes the subject; the past participle "delivered" (V3) becomes the simple past verb "delivered" (V2, same form here since "deliver" is a regular verb); and the object "the package" becomes the object of the active sentence, with "to the recipient's doorstep" retained unchanged.
◦ Active: The courier delivered the package to the recipient's doorstep.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it restructures the sentence around "the recipient" as the subject with "received", changing the focus and meaning of the original sentence (which is about the courier's action of delivering, not the recipient's act of receiving).

• Option 2 is incorrect because it is still in the passive voice ("was being delivered by") — merely changing the tense to past continuous passive, not converting it to active voice at all.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it is also still in the passive voice ("was delivered... by the courier"), with only the word order rearranged; it has not been converted to active voice.

NOTE

• A sentence is in the active voice only when the doer of the action (here, "the courier") is the grammatical subject performing the verb directly, without "by" or a form of "be + V3".

• Common trap in these questions: options that merely reorder a passive sentence, or change its tense/aspect, without actually converting it to active voice.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the underlined word in the following sentence.
The incorrigible optimism displayed by Aishwarya in difficult situations turned out her to be a favourite among her friends.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. unchanged (no replacement needed).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Incorrigible" literally means not able to be corrected or reformed, but when used with positive qualities such as "optimism", "enthusiasm" or "cheerfulness", it idiomatically means persistent, irrepressible or incurably strong in that quality — i.e., someone whose optimism cannot be dampened or changed. (अटूट/असुधार्य)
◦ Example: Despite repeated setbacks, his incorrigible optimism kept the whole team motivated.

• Here, "incorrigible optimism" correctly conveys that Aishwarya's optimism was so persistent that no difficulty could change or diminish it — this fits the context perfectly, so the underlined word should remain unchanged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Translucent" (पारभासी): Allowing light to pass through partially; semi-transparent. This describes a physical/visual property and makes no sense describing "optimism".

• Option 2: "Illustrious" (प्रतिष्ठित/यशस्वी): Well known, respected and admired for past achievements. While positive, it describes fame/reputation, not the persistent, unshakeable nature that "incorrigible" conveys here.

• Option 4: "Barefooted" (नंगे पांव): Without shoes on one's feet. This is entirely unrelated in meaning to "optimism" and makes no sense in the sentence.

NOTE

• "Incorrigible" is unusual in that it can carry a mildly humorous/affectionate positive sense ("an incorrigible romantic", "incorrigible optimism") in addition to its more common negative sense ("an incorrigible criminal") — SSC vocabulary questions sometimes test this context-dependent nuance.

• When none of the alternative options fit the sentence's meaning as well as the original underlined word, the correct choice is that no change is needed.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Climatic disasters are (1)________ increasingly common due to the effects of climate change. These disasters include extreme weather events such as hurricanes, tornadoes, floods and droughts. To mitigate the effects of these disasters, it is essential to invest in disaster preparedness and (2)________. The impact of climatic disasters is not limited to the loss of life and property damage. For example, hurricanes can disrupt the oil and gas industry, leading to higher fuel prices and (3)________. Floods can damage crops and infrastructure, leading to food shortages and disruptions to transportation systems. Rising temperatures can lead to more frequent heat waves, while changes in precipitation patterns can lead to more (4)________ droughts and floods. Climatic disasters disproportionately affect vulnerable populations. Collaboration among governments, communities and businesses is crucial for effective disaster preparedness and response. This involves investing in early warning systems, improving infrastructure and emergency services and planning for post-disaster recovery. By taking a (5)________ approach to disaster management, we can reduce the impacts of climatic disasters and build more resilient communities.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Becoming.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Climatic disasters are (1)________ increasingly common due to the effects of climate change." The verb structure already has the auxiliary "are" before the blank, so the blank must complete a Present Continuous construction: "are becoming", meaning the disasters are in the ongoing process of turning into something increasingly common.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense: Subject + is/am/are + V1+ing. Since "are" is already given, the blank must take the -ing form of the verb, i.e., "becoming".

• Applying the rule: "Climatic disasters are becoming increasingly common" correctly describes an ongoing trend, which fits the overall present-tense, ongoing-effects tone of the passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "became" is the simple past tense form; it cannot follow the auxiliary "are", which requires an -ing form, not a past-tense verb.

• Option 3: "become" is the base form; while it could follow "have" (present perfect) it cannot directly follow "are" to form a grammatically correct continuous tense.

• Option 4: "becomes" is the simple present, third-person singular form; it also cannot follow the auxiliary "are" in a continuous construction.

NOTE

• Always check the auxiliary verb already present before a blank (is/am/are, has/have, was/were) — it determines which form of the following verb (V1, V1+ing, V3) is grammatically required.

• "Are becoming" signals a trend that is currently developing, commonly used in academic/report writing to describe ongoing change — a useful pattern to recognise in cloze passages.

solution_text:

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "it is essential to invest in disaster preparedness and (2)________." The phrase "disaster preparedness and response" is a standard, commonly used collocation in disaster-management contexts, referring to the two complementary stages: getting ready before a disaster (preparedness) and acting during/after it (response).

• Rule — Contextual/collocation-based cloze: In cloze passages, the correct word often forms a fixed pair or commonly used phrase with a nearby word — here "preparedness and response" is a standard paired term, further supported later in the passage by the phrase "effective disaster preparedness and response."

• Applying the rule: "invest in disaster preparedness and response" fits both the immediate grammar and the passage's overall theme of managing disasters proactively and reactively.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "regeneration" refers to renewal or regrowth (e.g., of tissue, forests); it does not pair naturally with "preparedness" in a disaster-management context.

• Option 3: "evaluation" means assessment or judgement of value; while disasters may be evaluated afterward, this is not the standard paired term with "preparedness".

• Option 4: "manifestation" means an outward sign or expression of something; it does not fit the meaning of investing resources into disaster management.

NOTE

• Common disaster-management collocations tested in cloze passages: "preparedness and response", "early warning systems", "post-disaster recovery", "resilient communities" — all of which appear later in this very passage.

• In cloze passages, later parts of the passage (here, "effective disaster preparedness and response") often confirm or repeat the correct word choice used earlier — always scan the full passage before finalising an answer.

solution_text:

• The sentence reads: "hurricanes can disrupt the oil and gas industry, leading to higher fuel prices and (3)________." Since fuel supply is disrupted, the logical consequence — paired with "higher fuel prices" — is a shortage of fuel, i.e., insufficient supply to meet demand.

• Rule — Cause-and-effect cloze: The blank must logically continue the cause-effect chain set up in the sentence: disruption of the oil and gas industry → higher prices and reduced availability (shortages). Both effects (higher prices, shortages) are typical, commonly paired consequences of supply disruption.

• Applying the rule: "leading to higher fuel prices and shortages" is logically consistent, and mirrors the passage's later use of "food shortages" as a parallel consequence of floods — confirming "shortages" as the intended word.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

• Option 1: "fatigue" means extreme tiredness; it does not logically follow from a disruption to an industry or fuel prices.

• Option 3: "failure" (industry/system failure) is too strong and non-specific here; the sentence is about the economic consequence (prices and supply), for which "shortages" is the more precise and commonly used term.

• Option 4: "drought" refers to a prolonged shortage of rainfall/water — a distinct meteorological event already mentioned separately in the passage, and unrelated to fuel prices.

NOTE

• Notice the passage later uses the exact parallel phrase "food shortages" for floods — recognising this parallel structure helps confirm "shortages" as the answer for blank 3 as well.

• In cause-effect cloze sentences, look for a word that logically completes a chain that has already begun (here: disruption → higher prices → shortages).

A "proactive approach" means acting in advance/anticipation of a problem, rather than merely reacting after it occurs — which matches the passage's emphasis on early warning systems, preparedness and planning for recovery.

• Rule — Thematic consistency: The whole passage stresses preparing in advance (investing in preparedness, early warning systems, improving infrastructure) rather than only responding after disasters strike. "Proactive" is the word that best captures this forward-looking, preventive theme.

• Applying the rule: "By taking a proactive approach to disaster management" logically concludes the passage's argument that anticipatory planning (not just reaction) reduces the impact of climatic disasters.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "productive" means yielding good or useful results/output — it describes efficiency of output, not a forward-looking, preventive attitude towards disaster management.

• Option 3: "bioactive" is a scientific/chemical term describing a substance that has an effect on living tissue; it is entirely unrelated to disaster-management strategy.

• Option 4: "inactive" means not active or not functioning — this is the opposite of the passage's message of active preparedness and planning.

NOTE

• "Proactive" (anticipating and acting in advance) is frequently contrasted with "reactive" (responding only after an event has occurred) — a common vocabulary pair in SSC comprehension and vocabulary questions.
